messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Minh Tran was in his late sixties, his adult daughter was admitted to the hospital with a life-threatening obstetric complication. He still cannot tell the story in a straight line. He starts with the fluorescent lights, then the sharp antiseptic smell in the hallway, then the sight of staff rushing a gurney past him, and somewhere in the middle he loses the thread. What remains most vivid is not an ordered account but a set of scenes that return intact: his daughter pale and drenched in sweat, the monitor alarms, the words shouted between clinicians, the sense that both she and the baby might die before he could do anything. He remembers standing outside a treatment room while a procedure was being prepared, feeling as if the world had narrowed to the smell of disinfectant and the sound of metal trays being moved. Even now, what frightened him most was how quickly ordinary signs of birth became signs of catastrophe.

In the months after she survived, Minh found that reminders of that day did not stay in the past. A hospital corridor, the smell of antiseptic at a clinic, even passing a maternity display in a store and seeing infant clothes or pregnant women would grip him before he had time to think. His chest tightened, his hands shook, and a rush of fear and horror came over him with such force that he felt briefly disoriented, as if he were again outside that treatment room waiting to hear whether his daughter would live. At his own medical appointments he would become drenched in sweat while a nurse wrapped the blood pressure cuff around his arm, his body reacting as though he were back in that emergency, not in a routine exam for himself. The trigger was often enough to bring the whole experience crashing forward.

What comes back to Minh does so in a repetitive, cinematic way. He describes the memory as a film that plays over and over, but not like a story he is recalling from long ago. It arrives with the conviction of the present tense. When the antiseptic smell catches him off guard, he does not simply remember the hospital; for a few moments he feels he is there again, hearing the same alarms and waiting for the same terrible news. Pregnancy and babies have become potent in the same way. Seeing a newborn photograph sent by a coworker in his cybersecurity team can abruptly call up the delivery-unit scenes, and because those scenes return with such immediacy, he has come to scan for these reminders in places other people would not notice.

That scanning has slowly shaped his days. In his office, where he spends long hours monitoring incidents and evaluating system vulnerabilities, he now studies his environment for anything that might set him off: a message about family leave in the company chat, a colleague mentioning a grandchild, the medicinal odor that drifts in when the building’s clinic door opens. Because the memory feels current rather than finished, these cues seem dangerous to him, and he stays alert to them in meetings and break rooms. He chooses routes through the building that bypass the clinic corridor. He postpones his own appointments whenever he can. On one occasion, he left in the middle of a routine examination when the smell of disinfectant and the clatter of instruments made him feel as if the emergency was unfolding again.

The intensity of his reactions also seems to feed the memories themselves. Once his body surges into panic—heart racing, shoulders rigid, a sickened drop in his stomach—the images sharpen and replay more forcefully. He becomes certain, in those moments, that he is about to witness the same loss, and that certainty pulls him deeper into the scene until he is no longer grounded in the present. Afterwards he is ashamed by how completely he was overtaken, yet he cannot explain to others what happened without becoming confused and fragmented. He begins to recount a doctor entering the room, jumps to his daughter crying out, then stops, visibly lost, as if the memory has swallowed the words.

Widowed for years, Minh has lived alone with this pattern. He has kept functioning at work through discipline and routine, but the effort has become increasingly costly. He avoids team celebrations when coworkers bring infants to the office, delays preventive medical care, and feels humiliated by how quickly his body betrays him. What finally brought him to seek help was an episode during a recent physical, when the smell of antiseptic and the preparation for a minor procedure made him jerk back from the table and briefly feel he was once again waiting outside the room where his daughter might die. He left without completing the exam. Now, at 75, he says he is afraid that the memories will keep taking over whatever years he has left, and he wants, more than anything, to be able to enter a clinic or see a baby without feeling pulled back into that day.
